A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CKnowEdit and retain identifiable datasets, editors and research objectives. All 17 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including the illustrated appendices, support comparison. Revised evaluation settings prevent direct score comparisons but do not undermine document comparability.

before.justification: v1 reports original editing experiments on Qwen-7B-Chat and Baichuan2-7B-Chat in Table 1, with additional experimental cases in Figures 3 and 11–16.

after.justification: v2 reports original four-model editing results, translation and cross-language experiments, and human evaluation of its automatic scorer (Figures 4–6 and 14; Section 4.4).

M1.justification: The work remains a dataset and benchmark study without a new or revised proposed editing algorithm. No procedural changes to the retained editors are established. AlphaEdit changes the baseline set, while GPT-4o changes evaluation scoring.

E1.justification: v2 adds 94 history instances to the retained Chinese domains and introduces English editing through translation and English-to-Chinese transfer tests (Section 4.3). These substantially extend evaluated language conditions. Renaming Phonetic Notation to Pinyin and subdividing Ruozhiba into three logic categories largely reorganize existing coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparison removes PROMPT, adds AlphaEdit, and includes pre-edit model results. FT-M, AdaLoRA, ROME and GRACE remain, so most comparator membership is preserved (v1 Table 1; v2 Figure 4).

E3.justification: Both versions evaluate generated answers, but v2 replaces averaged ROUGE-L and embedding similarity with GPT-4o judgments, adds a separate rephrase-generalization metric, and drops standalone entropy-based fluency. It adds Qwen2-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-LLM-7B-Chat. New protocols use 100 samples per major category for translation experiments and 70 samples for human validation.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic translation comparisons using AdaLoRA and ROME, cross-language transfer failure cases, and human validation of the evaluator (Sections 4.3–4.4; Figures 5, 6 and 14). The earlier editor-specific monolingual cases in v1 Figures 3 and 11–16 are removed. This substantially changes the questions investigated by supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: v2 introduces correlation-based statistical validation between automatic and human ratings in Section 4.4; v1 contains no corresponding analysis. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v1's two-model results in Table 1 are replaced by four-model judge-based results in v2 Figure 4, including pre-edit and generalization scores. New findings include ancient-poetry portability mostly below 1, category-dependent translation effects, and automatic–human rating correlation of 0.70. These are substantial new or replaced results under changed conditions, rather than comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: v1's Background section defines the edit descriptor, edited model and likelihood-maximization objective. v2 removes this formalization. Neither version contains substantive theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution of a Chinese-specific editing benchmark and the conclusion that existing editors struggle are retained. v2 explicitly claims a 'first-ever' dataset for linguistic, factual and logical correction and promotes its revised evaluation as better aligned with real-world applications, providing limited additions to the contribution claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds mechanism hypotheses concerning AdaLoRA versus localized edits, rare characters and distribution shifts in poetry, and language-specific parameter regions. It interprets translation effects separately for linguistic, factual and logical knowledge and newly acknowledges category imbalance and judge bias. The earlier discussion of token overlap and dialect coverage is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds the GPT-4o evaluator version, scoring workflows and example prompts, GPU information, and detailed annotation checks including dual review and 20% calibration. However, v1's seven complete dataset-generation templates in Figures 4–10 are removed. This substantially changes reproducibility documentation; the stated EasyEdit code/data access remains unchanged.

R1.justification: The central positioning against English-centric and translated editing datasets persists. v2 adds references and discussion concerning AlphaEdit, WISE, NSE, MT-Bench and linguistic regions, while citations supporting the old metrics disappear. Its explicit 'first-ever' claim sharpens novelty positioning without replacing the underlying research premise.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and dataset narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 introduces a sourcing-criteria section and structured construction and quality-assurance subsections, moves Related Work after experiments, removes the formal Background and earlier Discussion, and adds standalone Limitations. The appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 expands the opening illustration into a category overview, redraws the construction diagram, separates dataset statistics, and replaces Table 1 with a four-model bar-chart grid. New radar plots and transfer cases accompany extensive replacement of appendix generation templates and experimental cases with dataset examples and evaluation diagrams.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential basis: translation and transfer experiments directly test its Chinese-specific motivation, pre-edit controls clarify editing effects, and human agreement provides validation of the new evaluator. More explicit annotation checks and limitations improve transparency. Losing generation templates and exact tabulated scores weakens reproducibility and precision, and Section 3.3's percentages conflict with Figure 3's updated counts. Nevertheless, the direct validation addresses central weaknesses of v1 and outweighs these reporting drawbacks.
